items.q: **HCM** stands for _______.
items.explain: **Human Capital Management** — the module SAP calls **[HR]**. The word *capital* is deliberate: it frames employees as an **asset to be developed**, not a cost to be minimised, which is why the chapter summary says HCM *"brings in a holistic treatment of employees."*

items.q: **EHS** stands for ________, *as the deck expands it*.
items.explain: The deck expands EHS as **Employee Health and Safety**, and that is the answer to give here. ⚠️ Be aware that **industry more commonly reads EHS as "Environment, Health and Safety"** — the deck's own sub-areas (industrial hygiene, occupational health, hazardous substances) belong to that broader reading. **Answer the deck.**

items.q: **HR processes can be grouped as ________ and ________.**
items.explain: **Strategic / core** processes versus **operational / routine** processes. The reliable test: **strategic processes contain "design" or "planning"** — *performance management process **design***, *compensation **planning***, *workforce **planning***. **Operational processes are the running of the thing** — records, leave, time, tax, payroll.

items.q: **Interviewing** is a part of the ERP ___________ management module.
items.explain: **Recruitment management.** The recruitment flow runs **requisition → sourcing → screening → interviewing → offer → onboarding**, and interviewing sits squarely inside it. Do not drift toward *talent management* — that starts once the person is already an employee.

items.q: **Labour tracking** is a part of the ERP ________ module.
items.explain: **Time and Attendance.** Labour tracking is the recording of *hours worked against what* — which is also the link into costing, since those hours become **activity cost** at the work centre's linked cost centre.

items.q: **True or False:** *"360-degree performance evaluation is a part of the ERP performance management module."*
items.explain: **TRUE.** Performance management explicitly lists *"performance measurements — direct / indirect inputs, **360 degree appraisals**."* **360-degree means feedback from all directions** — manager, peers, subordinates, sometimes customers — because in knowledge work your manager sees only a fraction of what you do.

items.q: **True or False:** *"Succession planning is a part of learning management."*
items.explain: **FALSE — succession planning belongs to Talent Management.** The two are adjacent and easy to confuse: **learning management delivers training**; **succession planning identifies who replaces whom** — a talent decision, not a training activity. *Skill training* also appearing under Talent Management is what makes the boundary slippery.

items.q: **True or False:** *"Employee self service is a part of personnel management."*
items.explain: **TRUE.** ESS is treated as part of the **personnel management** area, even though the HCM wheel draws *Employee Self Service* as its own segment. The employee portal — leave application, pay slip access, personal data maintenance — is personnel administration handed to the employee.

items.q: **True or False:** *"Planning job roles is a strategic HR process."*
items.explain: **TRUE.** It contains the word **planning** — the reliable marker for the strategic column. **Design it or plan it = strategic; run it every month = operational.**

items.q: **True or False:** *"Payroll is a strategic HR process."*
items.explain: **FALSE — payroll is operational / routine.** ⚠️ Note the deliberate pairing with the previous question: **compensation *planning* is strategic, but *payroll* is operational.** High volume, objective rules, run every month — which is also exactly why payroll was in the **first wave** of HR automation.

items.q: **True or False:** *"MRP stands for Management Resources Planning."*
items.explain: **FALSE.** **MRP = Material Requirement Planning.** The confusable neighbour is **MRP II = Manufacturing Resource Planning** — and note it is *Manufacturing*, not *Material*, and *Resource*, not *Requirement*. **Neither one is "Management."**

items.q: Which of these are things an **employee** does for themselves under **ESS**, per the deck? *(select all that apply)*
options: Accessing pay slip and payroll data
items.explain:
The deck's ESS list: **benefits, maintenance of personal data, leave application, accessing pay slip and payroll data, registering for a new training** — and *"employees maintain all these data and do all these transactions themselves."* **Budget approval is a manager/finance action, not self-service.**

The principle: **the person who knows your new address is you** — self-service moves data entry to whoever holds the knowledge.

items.q: Which of the following are given as **common examples of recruitment analytics**? *(select all that apply)*
items.explain: The QnA names exactly three: **cost per hire · time to fill vacant positions · onboarding efficiency.** Notice they measure **money, speed and quality of the hiring process** — attrition is a *retention* metric, measured after recruitment ends.

items.q: What are the **four broad categories of applications** under the financial module?
options: Financial Accounting · Management Accounting · Financial SCM · Treasury Applications
Accounts Payable · Accounts Receivable · General Ledger · Payroll
items.explain:
**Financial Accounting · Management Accounting · Financial Supply Chain Management · Treasury.** 

The cleanest way to hold them: **FA looks outward** (statutory, for regulators and investors), **MA looks inward** (for managers), **FSCM manages the cash cycle with customers and suppliers**, and **Treasury manages the money itself.**

items.q: Expand **AR**, **AP** and **GL**.
options: Accounts Receivable · Accounts Payable · General Ledger
Annual Return · Advance Payment · Gross Ledger
Asset Register · Asset Payable · General Ledger
Accounts Receivable · Advance Payable · Group Ledger
items.explain:
**AR = Accounts Receivable** (money customers owe you) · **AP = Accounts Payable** (money you owe suppliers) · **GL = General Ledger** (the book everything posts into — *trial balance, balance sheets, audit reports*).

**Direction check:** *Receivable = incoming, Payable = outgoing.* AR is the tail of **Order-to-Cash**; AP is the tail of **Procure-to-Pay**.

items.q: Which of the following fall under **Financial Accounting**, per the QnA? *(select all that apply)*
options: Accounts Payable — automating the Invoice-to-Payment cycle
Accounting GL — trial balance, balance sheets, audit reports
Product cost planning and profitability analysis
items.explain:
The QnA's areas under financial accounting: **AP (Invoice-to-Payment), AR / collection management (payment receipt, credit checks, risk management, customer service), and GL (trial balance, balance sheets, audit reports).**

**Product costing and profitability analysis are Management Accounting** — inward-facing, for managers, not statutory.

items.q: Expand **MRP**, **MRP II**, **SOP** and **MPS**.
options: Material Requirement Planning · Manufacturing Resource Planning · Sales and Operations Planning · Master Production Scheduling
Material Resource Planning · Manufacturing Requirement Planning · Standard Operating Procedure · Master Production Schedule
Manufacturing Requirement Planning · Material Resource Planning · Sales Order Planning · Material Planning Schedule
Material Requirement Planning · Material Resource Planning · Sales and Operations Planning · Master Planning Schedule
items.explain:
**MRP = Material Requirement Planning** · **MRP II = Manufacturing Resource Planning** · **SOP (S&OP) = Sales and Operations Planning** · **MPS = Master Production Scheduling.**

⚠️ **SOP here is NOT "Standard Operating Procedure"** — a genuine trap given how common that expansion is elsewhere.

items.q: Put the **five levels of MRP II** in order, from longest horizon to execution.
options: Business Plan → S&OP → MPS → MRP → Purchasing and Production Activity Control
S&OP → Business Plan → MPS → MRP → PAC
Business Plan → MPS → S&OP → MRP → PAC
MPS → Business Plan → S&OP → PAC → MRP
items.explain:
**Business Says Make More Products** — **B**usiness Plan → **S**&OP → **M**PS → **M**RP → **P**AC.

Each level is **more detailed and shorter-horizon** than the one above it: the business plan is agreed jointly by *Marketing, Production, Finance and Engineering*; S&OP plans **product groups**; MPS plans **finished products**; MRP plans **components**; PAC is the **implementation phase**.

items.q: **Purchasing and Production Activity Control** — what distinguishes the two halves?
options: Purchasing controls flow of materials from vendor to factory; production activity control plans and controls flow of work through the factory
Purchasing controls the budget; PAC controls the schedule
Purchasing is strategic; PAC is operational
Purchasing handles finished goods; PAC handles raw materials
items.explain:
Word for word from the QnA: *"While **purchasing controls flow of materials from vendor to factory**, **production activity control plans and controls flow of work through the factory**."*

**Materials coming in, work moving through.** Note the level-5 framing — this is *"the **implementation phase** of production planning and control systems"*, the boundary where **planning becomes execution**.

items.q: **S&OP** is a joint plan developed by which team, and it plans at what level of detail?
options: Sales and Marketing together — quantities of different **product groups** per period
Production and Engineering together — quantities of **individual finished products** per period
Finance alone — revenue targets per quarter
Sales alone — customer orders per week
items.explain:
*"This is a joint plan developed by **Sales and Marketing team together**. This plan details the quantities of different **product groups** that need to be produced in each period."*

**Product groups, not products** — that is the level-2 signature, and the distinction from **MPS**, which plans *finished products*. S&OP also does a **capacity availability check through Resource Planning (RP)**.

items.q: A **master production schedule** specifies
options: what product is to be made, and when
what component is to be made, and when
the financial resources required for production
the labor hours required for production
items.explain: **What product, and when.** ⚠️ Option B is the trap — **components are MRP's job, not MPS's.** MPS plans **finished products**; MRP explodes those into components.

items.q: The ______ is the MRP input detailing **which end items are to be produced, when they are needed, and in what quantities**.
items.explain: The **master production schedule**. Remember MRP's three inputs as three questions: **MPS** = *what must we build, and when?* · **BOM** = *what goes into it?* · **inventory records** = *what do we already have?*

items.q: A **master production schedule** contains information about
options: quantities and required delivery dates of **final products**
quantities and required delivery dates of all sub-assemblies
inventory on hand for each sub-assembly
inventory on hand for each final product
items.explain: **Final products.** Three MPS questions in a row all pivot on the same distinction: **MPS lives at the finished-product level.** Sub-assemblies appear only once **MRP explodes the BOM**.

items.q: In **continuous (make-to-stock)** operations, the master production schedule is usually expressed in terms of ______; in **job shop (make-to-order)** operations, in terms of ______.
items.explain:
**MTS → end-items · MTO → customer orders.** 

The logic is *what you can name in advance*: making for stock, you know the **product** but not the buyer, so you schedule **end-items**. Making to order, the **order itself** is the unit — every one is different. *(Assemble-to-order sits between them and is expressed in **modules**.)*

items.q: **Customer specific products** are also known as __________.
items.explain: **Make-to-order.** *Customer specific* is the giveaway — the product does not exist until a specific customer asks for it. Push it further and you get **engineer-to-order**, where *"every new order has a unique Bill of Material"* — which is precisely why **MRP is not appropriate** there.

items.q: The ______ is the MRP input which lists the **assemblies, sub-assemblies, parts and raw materials needed to produce one unit** of finished product.
items.explain: The **bill of materials**. Note the phrase **"one unit"** — a BOM is *per unit*, which is why you multiply it by the schedule quantity. *"In a sense, BOM is like a **recipe** for a dish!"*

items.q: A **bill of materials** lists the
options: components, ingredients, and materials required to produce an item
operations required to produce an item
times needed to perform all phases of production
items.explain: **Components, ingredients and materials.** ⚠️ Option B — *operations required* — is the **routing**, not the BOM. Hold the pair: **BOM = ingredients; routing = method.** A recipe needs both.

items.q: The **bill of materials** contains information necessary to
options: convert (explode) net requirements at one level into gross requirements at the next level
convert gross requirements into net requirements
calculate quantities on hand and on order
place an order to replenish the item
items.explain:
**Net at one level → gross at the next.** ⚠️ Option B is the near-miss: **gross → net is done by subtracting inventory on hand**, which needs the *inventory records*, not the BOM.

In the worked example: A's **net = 22**, so B's **gross = 22**. The BOM supplies the multiplier that carries requirement downward.

items.q: **"Exploding" the bill of materials** means
options: converting the bill of materials into components and raw material requirements
determining the net requirements for all the components
identifying the lead time of all the components
determining the various components' quantities that are already on hand
items.explain:
**Converting the BOM into components and raw material requirements** — *"break up the end product (parent) sequentially into its lower level components (children) down to fundamental components."*

⚠️ Option B is deliberately close: **netting is a separate step** from exploding. Explosion produces the **gross** requirement; subtracting stock produces the **net**.

items.q: A **material requirements plan** contains information with regard to all of the following **except**
options: the capacity needed to provide the projected output rate
quantities and required delivery dates of all sub-assemblies
quantities and required delivery dates of final products
inventory on hand for each final product
items.explain: **Capacity is the exception — MRP plans materials, not capacity.** This *is* its stated limitation: MRP is an **infinite planning tool** that *"assumes capacity is infinite."* Checking capacity is a separate step called **CRP**, which is why **closed-loop MRP** exists at all.

items.q: A **major strength of MRP** is its capability
options: to minimize labor hours used in production
items.explain: **Timely and accurate replanning.** This connects to the **planning horizon**: because MRP only plans a window, it must be **re-run as the window slides forward**. It is not a plan made once but a plan continually recomputed — and being able to redo it quickly and correctly is the strength.

items.q: A **material requirements plan** specifies
options: the quantity and timing of planned order releases
the quantities of the product families that need to be produced
the capacity needed to provide the projected output rate
the costs associated with alternative plans
items.explain:
**Quantity and timing of planned order releases.** ⚠️ Option B — *product families* — is **S&OP's** level, not MRP's. Option C is the capacity exception again.

MRP's outputs split by *make or buy*: **Purchase Requisitions** for bought items, **Planned Orders** for in-house items.

items.q: In the deck's **backward scheduling** formula, the purchase requisition date is the MRP date **minus** which three things? *(select all that apply)*
items.explain:
$$\textbf{PR date} = \textbf{MRP date} - \textbf{GR processing time} - \textbf{Vendor lead time} - \textbf{Purchasing processing time}$$

**Three delays, three subtractions.** The most-forgotten is the **first** — material arriving at the gate is not yet usable; it must be received, inspected and put away.

items.q: In the **time fences** table, which zone allows **no change at all**, and how far from the due date is it?
items.explain:
**Frozen, 1–2 weeks: no change.** Then **Firm** (2–4 wks, ±5%), **Full** (4–6 wks, ±10%), **Open** (6+ wks, ±20%).

**Mnemonic — Frozen, Firm, Full, Open: the further away, the freer you are.** The logic is **commitment** — material within two weeks is already ordered, delivered and possibly on the machine.

items.q: Match the **capacity technique** to the **planning level it checks**. Which pairing is correct?
items.explain:
**Every planning level has a matching capacity check:**

$$\textbf{S\&OP} \leftrightarrow \textbf{RP} \quad \textbf{MPS} \leftrightarrow \textbf{RCCP} \quad \textbf{MRP} \leftrightarrow \textbf{CRP} \quad \textbf{PAC} \leftrightarrow \textbf{CC}$$

**"Rough Cut" is named honestly** — at MPS level you check only the **critical resources**, because the plan itself is not detailed enough to justify more.

items.q: The __________ planning features of most ERP systems offer **both rough cut and detailed** capacity planning.
items.explain: **Capacity.** *Rough cut* = **RCCP** at MPS level; *detailed* = **CRP** at MRP level. But note the deck's candour: *"ERP's support for capacity management is a little indirect"* — it **evaluates** and **presents** the conflict; resolving it (overtime, subcontract, re-sequence) is largely a **human decision**.

items.q: In **closed-loop MRP**, if the capacity check says the plan is **not realistic**, where is the correction applied?
options: Back at MPS — change the finished-goods plan and re-run MRP
At MRP — reduce the component quantities
At PAC — re-sequence the shop floor
At the Business Plan — revise the long-term goals
items.explain:
**Back at MPS.** The deck: *"If the plan is not executable, then the production plan for finished goods needs to be **changed at the master production schedule (MPS) stage**, and a **fresh MRP run** is needed."*

**The constraint propagates upward** — if capacity cannot support the plan, you build fewer finished products, which changes what sales can promise. The word *"loop"* is literal: output feeds back to input.

items.q: Which are the **four critical master data elements** for production planning? *(select all that apply)*
items.explain:
All four — mnemonic **"My BOM Works Right"**.

They answer four different questions: **Material Master** = *what is it?* · **BOM** = *what goes into it?* · **Work Center** = *where is it made?* · **Routing** = *in what order?*

**What · what-from · where · in-what-order.**

items.q: The **work center** is closely linked to which object in the finance module?
items.explain:
**Cost center.** This is the **integration point between production and finance**: the work centre is where work physically happens, the cost centre is where cost is recorded — two views of the same organisational unit.

Without that link, manufacturing knows how long things took and finance knows what things cost, and **nobody can connect the two.**

items.q: In **process industry**, what plays the role that the **BOM** plays in discrete manufacturing?
items.explain:
**Recipe ⟺ BOM in process industry.** Same role — what goes in, in what quantity — different name and different tolerances.

The scenario's other distinctive requirement is **batch management**, and it exists because *"chemical properties may differ"* between batches: two batches of the same material are **not interchangeable**.

items.q: **Back flushing** — which production scenario is it associated with, and what does it do?
options: Repetitive manufacturing — record finished goods, then deduct BOM-consumed quantities automatically
Process industry — record each batch's chemical properties for traceability
Kanban / JIT — trigger delivery from demand source to supply source
Engineer-to-order — rebuild the BOM for each new order
items.explain:
**Repetitive manufacturing.** Back flushing **inverts the normal flow**: instead of issuing materials then producing, you **record the finished goods and work backwards through the BOM** to deduct what must have been consumed.

⚠️ **The trade-off:** it assumes the BOM is exactly right, so **scrap, rework and substitutions are invisible** to it. It buys speed with accuracy.

items.q: The term **Kanban** was originally conceived by which company, and what does it literally mean?
items.explain:
**Toyota**, and it literally means **"visual sign" or "visual card"**. In the **1940s** the cards were **paper notes pinned on a physical board**, used *"to create a transparent work process and reduce production waste."*

Recall from Unit 2 that **Kanban/JIT by Toyota** is one of the named **best practices** embedded in ERP packages, alongside **Wal-Mart's VMI**.

items.q: **Distribution Resource Planning (DRP)** is
options: a time-phased stock replenishment plan for all levels of a distribution network
a transportation plan to ship materials to warehouses
a shipping plan from a central warehouse to retail warehouses
material requirements planning with feedback loop from distribution centers
items.explain:
**A time-phased stock replenishment plan for all levels of a distribution network.** The key words are **time-phased** and **all levels** — the other options each capture only one slice.

**DRP is not part of the MRP II flow**, but it is *"an extension of MRP logic to the distribution network"*: requirements translate inward, **LDC → CDC → CWH → Factory**.

items.q: **MRP II** is accurately described as
options: MRP augmented by other resource modules
MRP with a new set of computer programs that execute on micro-computers
usually employed to isolate manufacturing operations from other aspects of an organization
items.explain:
**MRP augmented by other resource modules** — *"not just production, but considers other functions such as **capacity, financial, HR, supply chain, billing**."*

⚠️ Option D is the **exact opposite** of the truth: MRP II **integrates** manufacturing with the rest of the organisation. Option C is a hardware red herring — the change was in **scope**, not in the computer.

items.q: **Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) II** is
options: an advanced MRP II system that ties in customers and suppliers
severely limited by current MRP computer systems
items.explain:
**Ties in customers and suppliers** — the 2000s row: *"Extended ERP, ERP II — focussed on clients, **optimizing the whole business network, including suppliers and clients**."*

**Each decade adds one ring outward:** $$\textbf{Materials} \rightarrow \textbf{Factory} \rightarrow \textbf{Enterprise} \rightarrow \textbf{Network}$$

items.q: The extension of MRP which reaches **labor hours and machine hours, order entry, purchasing, and direct interface with customers and suppliers** is
items.explain: **ERP.** ⚠️ This question and the MRP II one are neighbours in the bank and easy to swap — the discriminator is **"direct interface with customers and suppliers"**, which reaches **outside the company**. MRP II stops at the factory wall; **ERP crosses it.**

items.q: Match SAP's module names: **FI-CO**, **MM**, **SD**, **PP**.
options: Financial Accounting & Controlling · Materials Management · Sales and Distribution · Production Planning
Financial Integration & Costing · Maintenance Management · Service Delivery · Product Planning
Finance & Compliance · Module Management · Supplier Data · Purchase Planning
Fixed Income & Cash Ops · Materials Master · Sales Desk · Plant Production
items.explain:
**FI-CO** = Financial Accounting + Controlling (the **external/internal split**, which is why the name is hyphenated) · **MM** = Materials Management · **SD** = Sales and Distribution · **PP** = Production Planning.

The deck's caveat: *"different ERPs may have different sets of modules, **but the core functionality of production, Finance, Warehouse, Inventory, Asset Management will be there in some form or the other**."*

items.q: In the *earlier vs now* table, **EAM** and **SRM** share an identical "earlier" column. What was it?
options: Quality Mgmt · Product Dev Project mgmt
items.explain:
**Procurement · Vendor payment · Vendor rating** — word for word the same for both, which is the sharpest illustration of the deck's repeated point that there is *"lots of overlap in functionality."*

Hence the real decision: *"a company has to carefully weigh whether to go for an enterprise app that is critical to its business, or go for an integrated ERP. **It is not an easy decision.**"*
